analysis.one_liner: Lets the President cap gasoline prices, tap the oil reserve, and ban Alaska oil exports.
analysis.headline: Introduced in March 2003 with three sponsors, the bill was sent to four House committees, never received a hearing or vote, and died when the Congress ended in January 2005.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would let the President set price caps on wholesale and retail gasoline to hold prices at or below their March 1, 2002 levels, with a $1 million fine per violation. It would let the President tap the Strategic Petroleum Reserve when high prices stem from anti-competitive conduct, require oil companies to hold minimum inventories, ban exports of Alaska North Slope oil, and direct Congress's formal opinion that OPEC's production quotas violate world trade rules and should be challenged at the WTO.
analysis.who_benefits: Drivers, farmers, small businesses, and manufacturers who buy gasoline, diesel, and home heating oil would pay no more than pre-2002 prices for a year if the President chose to impose caps, and would benefit from reserve releases and inventory rules that limit price spikes after supply disruptions.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Drivers and businesses that burn fuel

how_it_helps.text: Authorizes the President to cap wholesale and retail gasoline prices at or below their March 1, 2002 levels, with a $1 million fine for willful violations, for one year after enactment.

Expands Strategic Petroleum Reserve drawdown authority to cover price increases caused by anti-competitive conduct by foreign countries or by oil producers, refiners, and marketers, and requires a presidential report to Congress whenever crude exceeds $25 a barrel for more than 14 days.
Directs the Energy Secretary to set minimum inventory levels that oil producers, refiners, and marketers must maintain so unexpected supply disruptions cause less price volatility.
Repeals the authorization to export Alaska North Slope oil and re-imposes the export ban, keeping that oil in U.S. markets.
States Congress's sense that OPEC's coordinated production cutbacks are de facto price fixing prohibited by WTO rules, and urges the President to file a WTO complaint against oil-producing countries.

analysis.who_pays: Oil producers, refiners, and marketers would bear the cost: price caps could limit their revenue, the $1 million fines and minimum inventory rules impose compliance costs, and the Alaska export ban would close off foreign buyers for Alaska crude. Some compliance costs could be passed into prices, and caps set below costs can cause shortages.

drawbacks.text: A gasoline price cap set at March 2002 levels regardless of costs is the kind of price control that has historically produced shortages and lines at the pump, and the bill's own enforcement machinery (fines, injunctions) acknowledges sellers would have incentives to evade it.

The price cap authority is discretionary — the President is 'authorized' to issue caps, not required to — and the cap provision expires one year after enactment, so the bill's most dramatic benefit depends entirely on a future administration choosing to use it.
Minimum inventory requirements make oil companies hold more stockpiles than market conditions would justify, a real carrying cost that could be recovered in prices at the pump.

Banning Alaska oil exports could reduce flexibility for West Coast refiners and give foreign markets less reason to hold Alaskan crude, with the benefit to U.S. consumers uncertain in tight-supply periods.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For consumers facing a price spike, the bill offers direct relief: caps, reserve releases, and inventory rules all aim at the same target. But the design is blunt — a fixed March 2002 price level pays no attention to what crude actually costs to produce or import, and the 1970s price-control experience warns that caps below cost lead to shortages. The report-and-study provisions are sensible diagnostics, and the OPEC WTO provision is a statement of position rather than an action. On balance the bill is a consumer-protection measure whose strongest tool carries genuine supply risks if misused.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to four House committees and two subcommittees, and none of them ever acted on it, so it died silently when the 108th Congress ended in January 2005.

narrative.text: Rep. Peter DeFazio introduced the Gasoline Price Stabilization Act of 2003 on March 12, 2003, joined by Reps. Marcy Kaptur and Bernie Sanders.

The bill was referred to four committees — Energy and Commerce, International Relations, Ways and Means, and Resources — meaning four different committees would each have to act before it could reach the floor.
Within a week it was further referred to subcommittees on Energy and Air Quality and Energy and Mineral Resources, and no further action of any kind was recorded for the rest of the Congress.
No hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote on the bill appears in its action history through the end of the 108th Congress on January 3, 2005.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil producers, refiners, and marketers, and Alaska crude exporters, all better off with no price caps, fines, inventory mandates, or export ban taking effect.

for.name: Rep. Peter DeFazio
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and pushed for gasoline price caps, Strategic Petroleum Reserve releases, and a ban on Alaska oil exports.

against.name: Rep. Billy Tauzin
against.role: Chair, House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Chair of the lead committee of referral; the committee never held a hearing or markup on the bill.

against.name: Rep. Richard Pombo
against.what_they_did: Chair of a committee of referral covering the Alaska oil export ban; never acted on the bill.

against.name: Rep. Bill Thomas
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Chair of a committee of referral; never acted on the bill.

sides.party_line_note: Only three members sponsored the bill — two Democrats and one Independent — no Republican cosponsored it, and the Republican-led committees to which it was referred never took it up; no votes were ever recorded.

industries.note: The bill would cap the prices they can charge for gasoline at March 2002 levels, fine violators $1 million per violation, and require them to hold minimum inventories of crude and refined products. Their interest in killing the bill ran against consumers who pay pump prices.

industries.industry: Alaska North Slope oil producers and exporters
industries.note: The bill repeals the legal authorization to export Alaska crude and re-imposes the export ban, keeping that oil in domestic markets where it can moderate U.S. prices rather than flowing to Pacific Rim buyers.

The bill labels OPEC's coordinated production cutbacks de facto price fixing and urges a WTO complaint against oil-producing countries, targeting the practice the bill's findings blame for high gasoline and heating oil prices.

industries.industry: Gasoline and heating-oil consumers (drivers, farmers, small businesses)
industries.note: Consumer households and fuel-dependent businesses are the intended beneficiaries of the caps, reserve drawdowns, and inventory rules; the bill's findings specifically cite harm to consumers, farmers, small businesses, and manufacturers from rising oil prices.
